title: Out-of-Order Execution
summary: How hardware executes instructions as their operands become ready instead of in program order, and Tomasulo's algorithm that makes it possible.

slides.markdown:
In an **in-order** pipeline, instructions issue strictly in program order — if the instruction at the head stalls (say, a cache miss taking 200 cycles), every instruction behind it stalls too, even ones with nothing to do with the miss.

That's a huge waste: a later, fully independent ADD sits idle behind a load it doesn't depend on. **Out-of-order (OoO) execution** exists precisely to let independent instructions bypass a stalled one, extracting the ILP that in-order issue leaves on the table.

**Dynamic scheduling** means the hardware decides *at runtime* which instruction to execute next, based on which operands are actually ready — not the compile-time order the program was written in.

An instruction is issued to execute the moment its inputs are available and a functional unit is free, regardless of instructions ahead of it that are still waiting. This is the core mechanism that turns a stalled load from a whole-pipeline stall into a stall of just that one instruction and its dependents.

**Reservation stations** are small buffers, one per functional unit (or shared among a few), that hold an instruction along with its operands — or placeholders for operands not yet computed — until everything it needs is ready.

An instruction issues into a free reservation station immediately, freeing up the front end to keep fetching, even while the instruction itself waits there for its inputs to arrive. Once all operands show up, the reservation station fires the instruction to its functional unit — decoupling *when an instruction is fetched* from *when it actually executes*.

**Tomasulo's algorithm** (IBM 360/91) is the classic scheme most OoO cores descend from.

![Tomasulo's algorithm's data flow: reservation stations, a common data bus broadcasting results, and register status tracking](assets/tomasulo-dataflow.svg)

Instructions issue into stations tracking ready operands. A result broadcasts on the **CDB** to every waiting station at once — stalled instructions become ready the same cycle.

slides.markdown:
Executing out of order creates a problem: the *outside world* — interrupts, exceptions, register state — must still look like instructions completed **in program order**. The **reorder buffer (ROB)** holds every in-flight instruction's result until it can **commit** in original order, even though execution was out of order.

An instruction can finish long before it commits — it waits in the ROB. This is what makes precise exceptions possible ([exceptions-in-pipelines](exceptions-in-pipelines)): nothing is visible to software until it's that instruction's turn.

| | In-order | Out-of-order |
|---|---|---|
| Issue order | Program order | Data-ready order |
| Hardware needed | Simple | Reservation stations, ROB, wakeup/select logic |
| Achieved ILP | Limited by head-of-line stalls | Much higher — hides latency behind independent work |
| Power/area cost | Low | High — scheduling logic is expensive |

**How to decide:** OoO wins when workloads have unpredictable latencies (cache misses, variable-latency ops) worth hiding; in-order wins where area/power budgets are tight and predictable, in-order-friendly code dominates (many embedded and mobile efficiency cores).

Follow three instructions through Tomasulo's algorithm:

```
I1: F0 = F2 * F4      ; MUL, 6-cycle latency
I2: F6 = F0 + F8      ; ADD, needs F0 from I1
I3: F10 = F2 + F12    ; ADD, independent of I1/I2
```

**Cycle 1** — all three issue into reservation stations. I1's operands (F2, F4) are both ready, so it starts executing. I2's operand F0 isn't ready yet — its RS entry records "waiting on the tag that will produce F0" instead of a value. I3's operands are ready; since the adder is free, it starts executing immediately, *bypassing I2* in program order.

**Cycle 2** — I3 finishes and broadcasts its result on the common data bus (CDB); any reservation station waiting on I3's tag captures it. **Cycle 7** — I1 finishes its 6-cycle multiply and broadcasts F0 on the CDB. I2's reservation station, which has been snooping the bus, captures the value the instant it appears and executes on the next cycle — no separate register read step, no stall waiting for I1 to retire.

The key move: I3 finished **before** I2 even though I2 issued first — pure out-of-order completion driven by data readiness, not program order.

Tomasulo's original design (IBM 360/91) had a real gap: results broadcast on the CDB and updated registers **as soon as they were computed**, out of order. That's fine until an earlier instruction faults — say I1 divides by zero one cycle after I3 already wrote its result to a register. The machine's visible state is now a mix of "before I1" and "after I3", which is a state the program could never legitimately be in. Precise exception handling (the OS needs to know exactly which instruction faulted and that everything after it hasn't happened yet) becomes impossible.

The **reorder buffer** fixes this by adding a commit stage: instructions may *execute* and write their result out of order into the ROB, but they only update architectural (register-file/memory) state by **retiring in strict program order** from the ROB's head. If I1 faults, the ROB simply never lets I1 commit — everything after it in the ROB is squashed, regardless of how far it actually executed — and architectural state ends up exactly as if execution stopped at I1.

This is why every modern out-of-order core (x86, ARM, RISC-V implementations) pairs Tomasulo-style scheduling with a ROB — the scheduling gives you the parallelism, the ROB gives you a state model software can reason about.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: how deep is the window, really
slides.markdown:
Out-of-order execution is bounded by how many in-flight instructions the hardware can track at once, and that number is a real, disclosed design parameter. Recent high-performance cores run ROBs of roughly **200–500+ entries** (Apple's Firestorm/Everest cores and recent x86 cores in that range), letting the scheduler look far past a stalled instruction to find independent work.

A bigger ROB isn't free: every entry needs storage for the instruction's destination, exception state, and completion status, and the logic to find the oldest uncommitted instruction (the commit pointer) and to flush hundreds of entries after a misprediction scales with size. This is a direct trade-off against clock speed and power — which is exactly why in-order cores (see **superscalar-execution**'s pitfall slide) remain the right choice for power-constrained designs even though they leave measurable IPC on the table.

As a rule of thumb: window size only helps if there's independent work within it to find — pairing a huge ROB with poor branch prediction wastes most of that window on instructions that get squashed anyway.
